lesson_title: Profit, Break-even, Interest and Inflation: the Vetkoek Stall's Money Story
hook_text: Your stall opens at dawn already R300 in the hole. Vetkoek number 89 is the one that saves you — not 88.
clip_script: Fundraising stall, Bloemfontein. Batch of 100 vetkoek: flour 95, oil 120, filling 185, gas 60 — R460, so R4,60 each. Sell at R8: that's R3,40 profit a vetkoek — 73,9% on cost. Rich, right? Not yet. The market pitch cost R300, paid before the first customer. Every sale pushes R3,40 at that hole — not the full R8, because R4,60 of every sale walks straight back out for ingredients. So: 300 divided by 3,40 — 88,2. Sell 88 and you are STILL eighty cents down. Vetkoek 89 tips you into profit. Round up, always. Now the profit goes to the bank: R6 000 at 7%. Year one earns 420. Year two earns 449,40 — more, because the interest started earning interest. Year three: balance R7 350,26. But while your money climbs, so does the trolley: 6% inflation turns next year's R1 850 basket into R1 961. Budget on old prices and you are R111 short before the oil is hot. Two staircases, always racing. Make sure yours climbs faster.
visual_style: A dawn market stall with a glowing R300 pit beside it filling coin by coin, vetkoek 89 landing with a triumphant clink; then a split screen of two staircases — a bank balance climbing in green steps and a grocery trolley climbing in red.
mood: Entrepreneurial and urgent, the energy of a market morning where every sale counts.
pacing: Quick through the batch costing, a suspenseful crawl at 88 vetkoek, a beat of triumph at 89, then the steady climb of the two racing staircases.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and run any stall, sale or savings plan like a business.
